structs.name: Skin
structs.func: The body's largest organ and outer barrier. It keeps germs and water loss out, controls body temperature with sweat and blood flow, senses touch, heat and pain, and makes vitamin D.

structs.name: Deltoid
structs.func: The rounded muscle that caps the shoulder. It lifts the arm out to the side, and its front and back parts swing the arm forward and backward.

structs.name: Pectoralis major
structs.func: The big fan-shaped chest muscle. It pulls the arm across the body, rotates it inward and helps push things away, like in a push-up or a bear hug.

structs.name: Trapezius
structs.func: The large diamond-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck. It shrugs, squeezes and rotates the shoulder blades, and helps hold up the head and shoulders.

structs.name: Sternocleidomastoid
structs.func: The strap-like muscle running down each side of the neck. One side turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head; both together bend the neck forward.

structs.name: Biceps brachii
structs.func: The two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm. It bends the elbow and, most powerfully, turns the palm to face up, like turning a doorknob or screwdriver.

structs.name: Triceps brachii
structs.func: The three-headed muscle on the back of the upper arm. It straightens the elbow, powering pushing movements like push-ups, throwing and getting up from a chair.

structs.name: External oblique
structs.func: The largest and outermost flat muscle on the side of the belly. It bends and twists the trunk, holds the belly in, and squeezes the abdomen to help with coughing and breathing out hard.

structs.name: Gluteus maximus
structs.func: The biggest muscle in the body, forming the buttock. It powerfully straightens the hip for climbing, running and standing up, and helps keep the trunk upright.

structs.name: Quadriceps femoris
structs.func: The four-part muscle on the front of the thigh. It straightens the knee for standing, walking, kicking and jumping, and steadies the kneecap. One part also helps lift the thigh.

structs.name: Hamstrings
structs.func: Three muscles on the back of the thigh. They bend the knee and pull the thigh backward at the hip, and they brake the swinging leg when you run.

structs.name: Sartorius
structs.func: The longest muscle in the body, a thin strap that runs diagonally across the front of the thigh. It helps bend, lift and turn out the hip and bend the knee, like sitting cross-legged.

structs.name: Gastrocnemius
structs.func: The two-headed muscle that forms the bulge of the calf. It points the foot down to push off when walking, running and jumping, and also helps bend the knee.

structs.name: Soleus
structs.func: A broad, flat calf muscle lying under the gastrocnemius. It points the foot down and keeps you steady when standing, and squeezes leg veins to push blood back to the heart.

structs.name: Tibialis anterior
structs.func: The muscle along the front of the shin. It lifts the foot and toes up (dorsiflexion), stops the foot slapping down when you walk, and helps turn the sole inward.

structs.name: Skull (cranium)
structs.func: The bony case of the head. It protects the brain and the organs of sight, hearing, smell and taste, gives the face its shape, and has holes that let nerves and blood vessels pass in and out.

structs.name: Mandible
structs.func: The lower jaw bone, the largest and strongest bone of the face. It holds the lower teeth and moves at the jaw joints so you can chew, talk and swallow.

structs.name: Cervical vertebrae
structs.func: The seven neck bones (C1–C7). They hold up and move the head, protect the upper spinal cord, and carry the vertebral arteries up to the brain.

structs.name: Thoracic vertebrae
structs.func: The twelve vertebrae of the upper and middle back (T1–T12). Each one joins to a pair of ribs to form the back of the rib cage, protecting the heart and lungs and the spinal cord.

structs.name: Lumbar vertebrae
structs.func: The five big vertebrae of the lower back (L1–L5). They carry most of the upper body's weight, let you bend and straighten, and protect the bundle of nerve roots running to the legs.

structs.name: Sacrum
structs.func: A triangular bone at the base of the spine made of five fused vertebrae. It passes the weight of the upper body to the hip bones and legs and protects the sacral nerve roots that run to the pelvis and legs.

structs.name: Ribs
structs.func: Twelve pairs of curved bones that form the rib cage around the chest. They protect the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs and move up and out with each breath to help fill the lungs.

structs.name: Sternum
structs.func: The flat bone in the middle of the front of the chest. It anchors the collarbones and the upper ribs, completing the rib cage that shields the heart and great vessels.

structs.name: Clavicle
structs.func: The collarbone: a long S-shaped bone across the top of the chest. It acts as a strut that holds the shoulder out to the side so the arm can move freely, and it shields the nerves and vessels heading to the arm.

structs.name: Scapula
structs.func: The shoulder blade: a flat, triangular bone on the upper back. It forms the socket of the shoulder joint and anchors 17 muscles, gliding over the ribs so the arm can reach in almost any direction.

structs.name: Humerus
structs.func: The long bone of the upper arm, from shoulder to elbow. It forms the ball of the shoulder joint and the top half of the elbow, and anchors the muscles that lift, rotate and bend the arm.

structs.name: Radius
structs.func: The forearm bone on the thumb side. It rotates around the ulna so you can turn your palm up and down, and it carries most of the load from the hand into the forearm at the wrist.

structs.name: Ulna
structs.func: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. It forms the main hinge of the elbow with the humerus and stays fairly still while the radius rotates around it.

structs.name: Bones of the hand
structs.func: The 27 bones of the wrist and hand: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges. Together they make a flexible, strong framework for gripping, pinching and the fine movements of writing or surgery.

structs.name: Hip bone (pelvis)
structs.func: Each hip bone is formed by three fused bones: ilium, ischium and pubis. With the sacrum they make the pelvic ring, which carries body weight to the legs, forms the hip socket and protects the bladder and lower bowel.

structs.name: Femur
structs.func: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. It carries body weight from the hip to the knee, forms the ball of the hip joint and the top of the knee, and anchors powerful walking and running muscles.

structs.name: Patella
structs.func: The kneecap. It shields the front of the knee joint and acts like a pulley, giving the quadriceps more leverage to straighten the leg.

structs.name: Tibia
structs.func: The shinbone, the main weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. It carries body weight from the knee down to the ankle and anchors key muscles and ligaments.

structs.name: Fibula
structs.func: The thin outer bone of the lower leg. It carries little weight but anchors many muscles and forms the outer side of the ankle joint, keeping the ankle stable.

structs.name: Bones of the foot
structs.func: Twenty-six bones that form the foot's arches. Together they carry your full body weight, absorb shock with every step, and turn the foot into a stiff lever for pushing off.

structs.name: Frontal lobe
structs.func: The front part of each cerebral hemisphere. It plans and starts movements, controls speech production, and runs "executive" skills like decision-making, focus, self-control and personality.

structs.name: Precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex)
structs.func: The strip of brain just in front of the central sulcus that sends the commands for voluntary movement. Each part controls a specific body part on the opposite side of the body.

structs.name: Postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex)
structs.func: The strip just behind the central sulcus where body sensations first reach the cortex: touch, pressure, vibration, joint position, pain and temperature. Each part maps a body part on the opposite side.

structs.name: Parietal lobe
structs.func: The upper-middle part of each hemisphere. It processes touch and body position, combines senses to build a map of the space around you, and guides reaching. The left side also helps with reading, writing and math.

structs.name: Temporal lobe
structs.func: The lower side part of each hemisphere, behind the temples. It handles hearing, understanding language (on the left), recognizing faces and objects, and forming new memories with the hippocampus inside it.

structs.name: Occipital lobe
structs.func: The back part of each hemisphere and the brain's main vision center. It receives signals from the eyes via the thalamus and works out edges, colors, motion and shapes, with each side seeing the opposite half of the visual world.

structs.name: Insula
structs.func: A hidden lobe of cortex folded deep inside the lateral fissure. It senses the body's inner state (heartbeat, breathing, stomach, pain, temperature) and taste, and turns those signals into feelings and awareness.

structs.name: Cingulate gyrus
structs.func: A curved ridge on the inner surface of each hemisphere that wraps around the corpus callosum. It links emotion to action: it notices mistakes and conflict, adds the unpleasant feel to pain, drives motivation and supports memory.

structs.name: Parahippocampal gyrus
structs.func: A ridge on the inner underside of the temporal lobe next to the hippocampus. It is the main gateway into the hippocampus, carrying information in for memory, and it is key for recognizing places and scenes.

structs.name: Corpus callosum
structs.func: The largest bundle of nerve fibers in the brain, a thick C-shaped bridge joining the left and right hemispheres. It lets the two halves share information so they work as one brain.

structs.name: Hippocampus
structs.func: A curved, seahorse-shaped structure deep in the medial temporal lobe. It turns new experiences into lasting memories of facts and events and builds a mental map for finding your way.

structs.name: Amygdala
structs.func: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei deep in the front of the temporal lobe. It detects threats and emotionally important things, triggers fear and stress responses, and makes emotional events more memorable.

structs.name: Fornix
structs.func: An arching bundle of nerve fibers that carries the main output of the hippocampus forward to the mammillary bodies, thalamus and septal area. It is a key link in the memory circuit.

structs.name: Thalamus
structs.func: A pair of egg-shaped gray matter masses at the center of the brain. It is the main relay station that sorts and passes sensory signals (except smell) to the cortex, and it helps control alertness, attention and movement.

structs.name: Hypothalamus
structs.func: A small region below the thalamus that keeps the body in balance. It controls temperature, hunger, thirst, water balance, sleep and the stress response, and it directs the pituitary gland's hormones.

structs.name: Caudate nucleus
structs.func: A C-shaped nucleus of the basal ganglia curving alongside the lateral ventricle. It helps choose and start actions, learn from rewards and form habits, and links planning areas of the frontal lobe to movement.

structs.name: Putamen
structs.func: The outer part of the lentiform nucleus in the basal ganglia. It receives commands from the motor and sensory cortex and helps start, scale and smooth movements, and it stores well-practiced motor habits.

structs.name: Globus pallidus
structs.func: The inner, paler part of the lentiform nucleus in the basal ganglia. It is the main output 'brake' of the basal ganglia, holding back unwanted movements and releasing the chosen ones through the thalamus.

structs.name: Ventricular system (lateral, third and fourth ventricles)
structs.func: A connected set of fluid-filled spaces inside the brain. The choroid plexus in them makes cerebrospinal fluid, which flows through and around the brain and spinal cord to cushion them, carry away waste and keep pressure steady.

structs.name: Midbrain
structs.func: The top part of the brainstem. It controls eye movements and pupil size, relays hearing and vision reflexes, and holds the substantia nigra, which helps start smooth movement.

structs.name: Pons
structs.func: The bulging middle part of the brainstem. It relays signals from the cortex to the cerebellum, helps control breathing rhythm and sleep, and holds the nuclei for chewing, facial movement, outward eye movement and balance.

structs.name: Medulla oblongata
structs.func: The lowest part of the brainstem, joining the brain to the spinal cord. It runs life-support reflexes like breathing rhythm, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing and vomiting, and it is where most motor fibers cross sides.

structs.name: Cerebellum
structs.func: Coordinates movement, balance and posture, and fine-tunes the timing and accuracy of every movement. It also helps with motor learning, like getting better at a skill with practice.

structs.name: Spinal cord
structs.func: The main cable between the brain and the body. It carries movement commands down and sensations up, and it runs fast reflexes on its own, like pulling your hand off something hot.

structs.name: Optic nerve, chiasm and tract
structs.func: Carries vision from the eyes to the brain. At the optic chiasm, fibers from the inner half of each retina cross over, so each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the world.

structs.name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
structs.func: Moves most of the eye muscles, letting the eye look up, down and inward, and lifts the upper eyelid. It also carries signals that shrink the pupil and focus the lens for near vision.

structs.name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
structs.func: Controls one eye muscle, the superior oblique, which helps the eye look down and inward and rotates it inward. You use it when you look down to read or walk downstairs.

structs.name: Ophthalmic nerve (trigeminal V1)
structs.func: The top branch of the trigeminal nerve. It carries touch, pain and temperature from the forehead, scalp, upper eyelid, eye and the top of the nose, and it starts the blink reflex when your eye is touched.

structs.name: Heart (overview)
structs.func: A muscular pump in the middle of the chest with four chambers. The right side pumps blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the whole body, about 100,000 beats a day.

structs.name: Right atrium
structs.func: The upper right chamber of the heart. It collects oxygen-poor blood returning from the body through the venae cavae and passes it to the right ventricle. It also holds the SA node, the heart's natural pacemaker.

structs.name: Right ventricle
structs.func: The lower right chamber of the heart. It pumps oxygen-poor blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs, where the blood picks up oxygen and drops off carbon dioxide.

structs.name: Left atrium
structs.func: The upper left chamber of the heart. It receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.

structs.name: Left ventricle
structs.func: The heart's strongest pumping chamber. It squeezes oxygen-rich blood out through the aortic valve into the aorta, pushing it to every part of the body.

structs.name: Mitral valve
structs.func: A two-leaflet door between the left atrium and left ventricle. It opens to let oxygen-rich blood fill the ventricle and slams shut when the ventricle squeezes, so blood can't leak backward into the lungs.

structs.name: Tricuspid valve
structs.func: A three-leaflet one-way door between the right atrium and right ventricle. It lets used, oxygen-poor blood from the body fill the right ventricle and shuts when the ventricle pumps, stopping backflow.

structs.name: Aortic valve
structs.func: A three-cusp one-way valve at the exit of the left ventricle. It opens to let the ventricle pump blood into the aorta and snaps shut afterward so blood can't fall back into the heart.

structs.name: Pulmonary valve
structs.func: A three-cusp one-way valve at the exit of the right ventricle. It opens to let oxygen-poor blood flow into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs, then closes so it can't flow back into the heart.

structs.name: Coronary arteries
structs.func: The arteries that feed the heart muscle itself. They branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve and wrap around the heart, delivering the oxygen and fuel it needs to keep beating.

structs.name: Aorta
structs.func: The body's largest artery. It carries oxygen-rich blood from the left ventricle and, through its many branches, delivers it to the head, arms, organs and legs. Its stretchy wall also smooths out each heartbeat's pulse.

structs.name: Pulmonary trunk and arteries
structs.func: The short trunk and its two branches that carry oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. There the blood drops off carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. They're the only arteries that carry oxygen-poor blood after birth.

structs.name: Superior vena cava
structs.func: The large vein that returns oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest to the right atrium of the heart. It's the top of the two main veins feeding the heart.

structs.name: Inferior vena cava
structs.func: The body's largest vein. It returns oxygen-poor blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen up to the right atrium of the heart, running to the right of the aorta along the back of the abdomen.

structs.name: Carotid arteries
structs.func: The main arteries running up each side of the neck. They deliver most of the blood to the brain, eyes, face and scalp, and sensors in their walls help control blood pressure and breathing.

structs.name: Vertebral and basilar arteries
structs.func: The back blood supply of the brain. The two vertebral arteries climb through the neck bones and join into the basilar artery, which feeds the brainstem, cerebellum, inner ear and the back of the brain.

structs.name: Middle cerebral artery
structs.func: The largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It supplies the outer side of each brain hemisphere, including the areas for movement and feeling in the face and arm, and, on the dominant side, language.

structs.name: Subclavian artery
structs.func: The main artery to each arm. It arches over the top of the lung beneath the collarbone and also gives branches to the brain (vertebral artery), neck, shoulder and front chest wall.

structs.name: Brachial artery
structs.func: The main artery of the upper arm. It carries blood from the armpit down to the elbow, where it splits to supply the forearm and hand. It's the artery used when blood pressure is measured with a cuff.

structs.name: Femoral artery
structs.func: The main artery of the thigh. It carries blood from the groin down the leg to the knee, supplying the thigh muscles and continuing on to feed the lower leg and foot. Doctors often use it to thread catheters to the heart and brain.

structs.name: Hepatic portal vein
structs.func: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach, intestines, spleen and pancreas to the liver. The liver gets first pick of what was absorbed, processing nutrients and clearing toxins before the blood reaches the rest of the body.

structs.name: Internal jugular vein
structs.func: The main vein draining the brain, face and neck. It carries used blood from inside the skull down the side of the neck to join the subclavian vein and return to the heart.

structs.name: Great saphenous vein
structs.func: The longest vein in the body. It runs just under the skin from the inner side of the foot up the inner leg and thigh, draining the skin and fat of the leg into the deep femoral vein near the groin.

structs.name: Renal arteries
structs.func: Carry oxygen-rich blood from the aorta to each kidney. About a fifth of everything the heart pumps goes through them, so the kidneys can filter the blood and keep salt, water and blood pressure balanced.

structs.name: Lungs
structs.func: Bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide. Air reaches about 300–500 million tiny air sacs (alveoli), where gas crosses a wall thinner than a soap bubble into the capillaries.

structs.name: Trachea
structs.func: The windpipe: a stiff but flexible tube that carries air from the larynx down to the lungs. C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open, and its sticky, hair-lined lining traps dust and sweeps it back up.

structs.name: Bronchi
structs.func: Branching airways that carry air from the trachea into each lung, splitting again and again into smaller tubes. Their muscle can tighten or relax to control airflow, and their lining cleans the air.

structs.name: Larynx
structs.func: The voice box at the top of the windpipe. It holds the vocal folds that make sound, and it guards the airway: it closes tight when you swallow and triggers a cough if anything goes down the wrong way.

structs.name: Pharynx
structs.func: The throat: a muscular tube behind the nose and mouth shared by air and food. It carries air to the larynx and pushes swallowed food into the esophagus, with tonsils guarding the entrance against germs.

structs.name: Diaphragm
structs.func: The main muscle of breathing: a dome-shaped sheet between the chest and abdomen. When it contracts it flattens, enlarging the chest so air rushes into the lungs; it also helps with coughing and straining.

structs.name: Tongue
structs.func: A muscular organ in the mouth that moves food while chewing, shapes it into a ball and pushes it back to swallow. It also carries taste buds and is essential for clear speech.

structs.name: Salivary glands
structs.func: Make saliva, about 1–1.5 litres a day, which moistens food, starts digesting starch, protects the teeth and fights germs. The three big pairs are the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands.

structs.name: Esophagus
structs.func: A muscular tube that carries swallowed food and drink from the throat to the stomach using waves of squeezing (peristalsis). A sphincter at the bottom stops stomach acid from flowing back up.

structs.name: Stomach
structs.func: A stretchy muscular bag that stores food, churns it with acid and enzymes into a soupy mix called chyme, and releases it slowly into the small intestine. Its acid also kills many germs.

structs.name: Duodenum
structs.func: The first part of the small intestine, a C-shaped tube that receives food from the stomach plus bile and pancreatic juice. Here acid is neutralised and most chemical digestion begins.

structs.name: Jejunum and ileum (small intestine)
structs.func: The long, coiled middle of the gut where most nutrients are absorbed into the blood. The jejunum takes up most sugars, proteins and fats; the ileum reclaims bile acids and vitamin B12.

structs.name: Appendix
structs.func: A small, finger-shaped tube hanging off the caecum. It holds immune (lymphoid) tissue and may act as a safe store of helpful gut bacteria. When it gets blocked and inflamed, that's appendicitis.

structs.name: Colon (large intestine)
structs.func: The large intestine absorbs water and salts from leftover food, turning liquid waste into solid stool. It also houses trillions of helpful bacteria that ferment fibre and make some vitamins.

structs.name: Rectum
structs.func: The last part of the large intestine, which stores stool until it's a good time to empty the bowel. Stretch sensors in its wall tell you when it's filling, and muscles keep it closed until you decide.

structs.name: Liver
structs.func: The body's chemical factory: it processes nutrients from the gut, stores energy as glycogen, makes bile and blood proteins (like albumin and clotting factors), and breaks down old red cells, hormones and medicines.

structs.name: Gallbladder
structs.func: A small pear-shaped sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile. When you eat a fatty meal it squeezes, sending bile into the duodenum to help digest fat.

structs.name: Pancreas
structs.func: A gland behind the stomach with two jobs: it makes digestive juice full of enzymes and bicarbonate for the duodenum, and its islets release insulin and glucagon to control blood sugar.

structs.name: Kidneys
structs.func: Filter the blood to remove waste and extra water as urine. They also keep salt, potassium, acid and blood pressure in balance and make hormones that build red blood cells and activate vitamin D.

structs.name: Ureters
structs.func: Two thin muscular tubes that carry urine from each kidney down to the bladder. Waves of muscle squeezing push urine along, and a one-way valve stops it flowing back up.

structs.name: Urinary bladder
structs.func: A stretchy muscular bag that stores urine from the kidneys until it is a good time to empty it. The brain and spinal cord control when its wall squeezes and its sphincters open.

structs.name: Pituitary gland
structs.func: A pea-sized gland under the brain, often called the master gland. It releases hormones that control growth, the thyroid, the stress response and how much water your kidneys keep.

structs.name: Pineal gland
structs.func: A tiny gland deep in the middle of the brain that makes melatonin, mostly at night. Melatonin tells the body it is dark, helping set the daily sleep–wake rhythm.

structs.name: Adrenal glands
structs.func: Two small glands sitting on top of the kidneys. Their outer layer makes cortisol and aldosterone for stress, blood sugar, salt and blood pressure; their core makes adrenaline for the fight-or-flight response.

structs.name: Thyroid gland
structs.func: A butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. It makes thyroid hormones that set how fast your body burns energy, and they matter for growth, brain development, heart rate and body temperature.

structs.name: Spleen
structs.func: A fist-sized organ in the upper left abdomen that filters the blood. It removes old or damaged red blood cells, stores some blood cells and platelets, and fights germs in the blood, especially encapsulated bacteria.

structs.name: Thymus
structs.func: A gland behind the sternum (chest bone) where T cells, a key type of white blood cell, are trained. It teaches them to attack germs but not your own body. It is largest in childhood and shrinks into fat in adults.
